In summary, our research is concerned with
the intrinsic complexity of learning problems and the characterization of the most difficult learning problems.

the following questions: (1) What makes a class of languages the hardest one to be learned? (2) How can one measure hardness of learning? (3) What are natural classes of languages that are complete for the hardest degrees?

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the intrinsic complexity of learning from texts is characterized by a rich hierarchy of natural complete classes, where each class contains “multidimensional languages,” which are learnable from one another.
, in the limit, learning languages from texts can be as hard as solving any algorithmic problem.
“the more dimensions the language has and the more complex the learning strategy, the harder the language is to learn.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the intrinsic complexity of learning from texts can be quantified and characterized, and that this quantification and characterization is useful for studying the hardness of classes of languages.

the complexity of learning languages in the limit is determined by the intrinsic complexity of languages, and that the complexity of classes of languages is determined by the complexity of their learning problems.
we have obtained the most complete picture of learning in the limit by strategies of varying hardness and of the hardest classes of learnable languages.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the complexity of learning is not just a property of the language class but also depends on the learning strategy.

the complexity of language learning can be quantified in terms of intrinsic reductions between learning problems and that this complexity is related to the algorithmic and topologic potentials of the learning classes.
the intrinsic complexity approach to the study of learnability is a viable and useful alternative to other approaches.
